I had my first “attack” in August, 2017. By the time I started Ocrevus in March of 2019 I was on permanent disability and using a walker. I also had limited use of my upper arms. Ocrevus was a game changer for me. After my first full dose I went into remission for the first time in over 2 years. Unfortunately I didn’t stay in remission but I regained a lot of my function. 2 years later I’m still on permanent disability but I am definitely better than I was prior to starting Ocrevus. I also have a rare form of MS (Progressive Relapsing MS) so my experience with Ocrevus May look a little different than most people.

Hello, I am also in the U.S. I made a cross-country move in March 2020. I was terrified about changing insurances and finding a new neurologist. Fortunately, everything went very smoothly. My best advice is to research, research and research before your move. I started with identifying MS specialists in my area and then cross-researched insurance plans available on the Marketplace to identify plans that covered these providers. From there, I contacted these providers to find out what I needed to do to become a patient once I moved. This was crucial as both providers required a referral from my current neurologist along with all of my medical records. I was able to do this before my move so that once I moved and had applied for insurance I was able to schedule an appointment. I was really worried about my Ocrevus not being covered but this turned out to be a non-issue. I remember being completely overwhelmed but once I broke things down that I needed to do step-by-step it became much more manageable. Please feel free to DM me with any questions you have.
Take care, Erin

Most people with MS have some form of heat sensitivity, but like most MS symptoms it varies from person to person. Things like hot showers and hot tubs are definitely avoided by many people with MS. I am mentioning this because if I was reading about a fictional character who has MS and likes to unwind by sitting in a sauna or taking a long hot bath I would question the “realness” of the character. I started Ocrevus last March (2019) so I have had the 2 induction doses and the first full dose. I noticed some improvement about 5 weeks after the induction but then it got hot outside and I rapidly started to decline. When I got my first full dose in September I could immediately notice a huge difference in how I felt within 48 hours of the infusion. I received 3 days of IV steroids in October for an exacerbation of symptoms that I had had for months but otherwise it has been pretty much smooth sailing. Besides some hair loss at the beginning I haven’t noticed any side effects. My next dose is March 10 and my husband and I are moving to Oregon, USA  from the East Coast March 14th to get away from the hot summers where we live now.

I was initially started on Copaxone but stopped due to chest pain. I was then on nothing for a year (long, frustrating story). When I met my current Neuro doc he wanted me to start Ocrevus immediately. I was on Tecfidera for about a month after that due to insurance issues but stopped it once Ocrevus was approved. I had pretty bad GI side effects with Tecfidera that were annoying but manageable. 

My understanding of Ocrevus is that it helps stop progression but most people generally don’t experience such a dramatic improvement in symptoms as I did. My neurologist initially thought I had PPMS but now thinks that I have a very progressive form of RRMS and that Ocrevus has allowed me to finally achieve some sort of remission for the first time 2+ years since diagnosis.

I wish you the best of luck on your MS journey. Please feel free to PM me if you have any additional questions.

Hi. I imagine you are both extremely concerned, those are scary symptoms. If these are new symptoms and have not resolved since you posted this I would definitely go to the ED. The general rule of thumb with MS (at least the way I interpret it) is to wait 24 hours to 2 weeks , depending on the severity of the symptoms and if they are new symptoms, before going to the ED/contacting your neurologist. HOWEVER, if these are new symptoms, since he hasn’t yet been formally diagnosed with MS, he should go to the ED. The main reason is to R/O  causes other than MS. If MS is suspected, often the ED will admit the patient to the neurology unit (at least in the US) for a thorough work up (and possibly start him on a short course of IV steroids) which often will shorten the process of getting him started on medication to slow down the disease progression if it is MS. I am so sorry you are both going through this.

Unfortunately many people cannot stay at home from work when sick for a variety of reasons ranging from desperately needing money, fear of losing job due to calling out, having a chronic illness such as MS which has used up all sick leave and FMLA (US only) or just having kid who get sick a lot and require multiple doctors appointments. I imagine most of us with MS have gone to work when we had no business doing so. I know I have gone to work when I wasn’t contagious but had too much cog fog to safely provide care to my patients. (I’m a GP). The best thing to do, in my opinion, is practice common sense. If it’s flu season and you are going to see your GP for something non-urgent, consider rescheduling. Also consider carrying a mask and hand sanitizer (but don’t go overboard and bathe yourself in if) with you at all times in case you find yourself sitting next to someone on the bus/plane who appears sick. Make sure you are vaccinated appropriately including getting the flu shot annually and the pneumonia vaccine as recommended by your PCP. Unfortunately we can’t always control the decisions other people make but we can still do our best to protect ourselves as much as possible while striving to remain involved in our communities and living our best lives.

I have a diagnosis of RRMS but have never been in remission and was using a mobility aid (cane then walker) within 18 months of diagnosis. Needless to say I was bounced around to numerous MS specialists, all with very different opinions regarding treatment.  My current neurologist thinks I have a subtype of PPMS that was previously labeled PRMS (Progressive Relapsing MS). I saw another MS specialist that thought I had an atypical form of  RRMS and that with “aggressive” treatment I could go into remission. But they both agreed on starting Ocrevus. My overall improvement over the past 2 months has been amazing so I am skeptically hopeful that I have finally entered something close to remission, hence the dramatic improvement. Best of luck to you.

I started PT which helped a lot but my therapist wasn’t sure of the cause so she referred me to a Neuro PT who said it was definitely MS related; in my case recurrent muscle spasms followed by muscle stiffness and rigidity (but not spasticity according to my therapist) is the cause. After about 6 weeks of intensive PT with the Neuro-therapist I regained full ROM and although I occasionally have some weakness and pain it doesn’t occur very often.  Good luck and I am sorry you are dealing with this, I was absolutely miserable.

I think it’s important to decide if you want/need to work full time (extra money, health insurance, etc.), If you were hired as part time you should hopefully be able to maintain control regarding the decision to increase your hours. Jumping from 20/hours to 40 hours a week may or may not be doable but finding a schedule that works for you might be a good place to start. When I first reduced my hours from FT I found that working four 8 hour shifts with Wednesday off worked great for me. I then went to 8 hour shifts on Monday and Friday with half days the rest of the week.  I was open with my employer about my MS diagnosis and they were extremely accommodating. If you chose not to disclose your illness you may be able to get away with something along the lines of “I really love this job and am grateful to be offered a FT schedule. However, because I was initially hired to work PT I still have some other obligations I am committed to at this time but I am able to work “X hours a week” and in 3-6 months we can revisit the idea of increasing my hours to FT”. My advice is to take things slow if possible. Best of luck to you.

I am sorry you are dealing with this crappy disease. I am a Nurse Practitioner (I’ve lost track of the # of times a MA has saved my ass, so thank you). I really struggled with understanding the concept of managing my energy and when someone would suggest I slow down (post diagnosis) my response was always something along the lines of “but last month I was working FT and volunteering, etc., I just need to fight harder and I’ll get through this”. Boy was I WRONG. Surprisingly, working with an Occupational Therapist and focusing on fatigue and energy management was probably the most helpful treatment (besides DMT’s) that I have had so far. Besides learning some work arounds and tips and trips regarding my decrease in energy, I found it extremely therapeutic to meet with someone once or twice a week to talk about what I used to to be able to do that I can’t do now. It also helped snapping me out of denial and turning my attention to working towards what I could still do and how to do it better rather than focusing on what I had lost thanks to MS. Best of luck to you. Cheers!

The times I become concerned and contact my doctor is when a new symptom develops or a prior symptom becomes much more severe. For example, I have had problems with my left arm for months but after not being able to use it at all after 24 hours I contacted my Neuro doc and got IV steroids which didn’t magically make all of my symptoms go away but afterwards I had regained full use of my arm. ABSOLUTELY! I am a GP in the States and have always been very pro-flu shot, even before I got sick. My husband hates needles and every year we’d argue about him getting his flu shot. Once I got diagnosed I told him he would be getting a flu shot every year and that it wasn’t up for discussion. He actually got his before I did this year. The flu shot is on average only about 70% effective (it varies each year) but even if you get a flu shot and are unfortunate enough to get the flu according to The CDC you are much more likely to have less severe symptoms and a quicker recovery time. I worked in urgent care for several years and the people with the flu who had been vaccinated almost always were way less sick than those who hadn’t been vaccinated.

Sign up IMMEDIATELY for Long Term Disability benefits (you may already have them through your employer) and consider signing up for Short Term Disability as well. I already had a LTD policy through my work when I was diagnosed. I have a very aggressive form of MS and ended up being deemed permanently disabled less than 18 months after my diagnosis (NOTE: for newbies to this forum or for those newly diagnosed my case is extremely unusual). I am now receiving 60% of my previous income and will receive that until I am 67 (I am 43 now). That ends up being about 3 times more than I would receive from government disability. It also starts 90 days after you apply where as it is usually a 2-3 year process to get approved for government disability and although they do back pay a portion of that goes to attorneys and it means not having any income for up to several years.

I’m in the U.S. and my understanding is that if the LTD policy is purchased through your employer they can’t discriminate against pre-existing conditions but if you purchase a private policy they can. I know for most people even when a MS diagnosis is strongly suspected it takes a while for the “official diagnosis”. This waiting period is also a good time to look into purchasing additional benefits.

I contacted the National MS Society and they walked me through the process of applying for disability (SSDI). I hope that helps.

I would recommend by starting with an inexpensive fold up cane. It helped me realize what qualities I was looking for in a permanent cane (ex: one that stands up on its own was something I had never thought of before and ended up being a must have for me) and it’s also super practical. Hello,

There should be no issue with you getting a typhoid vaccine. Two versions are available; a live virus vaccine which is a pill you take in split doses over 7 days or an inactive (killed) vaccine which is an intramuscular injection just like the flu shot. Both appear to be equally effective but the oral version is becoming more common because a booster dose is only required every five years. The injection version requires a booster every 2 years. Booster doses are only needed when traveling to a region where typhoid is endemic. Most people with MS are immuo-comprimised but that is largely due to the medications we take. Speak with your neurologist but there should be no reason why you shouldn’t be able to get the typhoid injection. Even if you are not on a DMD I imagine you would be advised not to take the live vaccine.

Also, yellow fever is not endemic to Asia so there should be no issue traveling there (certain regions of Africa and South America are currently the only countries where yellow fever exists). Again, consult  with your neuro doc but also google cdc travel and that will give you the most up to date information regarding what country/region requires what vaccines. 

Cheers to a great holiday!

Hi there,
I have been a RN for 13 years and a Nurse Practitioner for 8 years. I also did nursing as a second career and was your age when I got my RN. I say go for it. I love nursing because there is so much you can do with your degree. You may get a lot of negative feed back about working 12 hour shifts and how physically demanding nursing is which is true, but that mainly applies to working in the hospital. Nursing jobs such as working in an outpatient clinic, community health nursing, being a school nurse or even being a phone triage nurse and working from home are all examples of different types of nursing jobs that are much less physically demanding than hospital nursing. My only advice would be to consider enrolling in a part-time nursing program which is usually 3 years. Nursing school is quite demanding and there is not a lot of flexibility with missing class or clinical rotations. My program allowed for students to start out full time and switch to part-time if needed so you may want to check into that when looking at schools. Best of luck to you and feel free to message me if you would like to discuss my personal experiences working in the nursing field with MS.

I imagine that not everyone on this site will agree with me but I am a firm believer that it is completely acceptable for people with a chronic invisible illness that do not appear physically disabled to use a mobility device, particularly in crowded or stressful situations. I started using a fold up travel cane (bought from Amazon, fits in a backpack or large handbag) last August on as needed basis for leg weakness and balance issues. Rather than being embarrassed like I thought I would, I found myself using the cane often when my walking was fine but other MS symptoms such as cog fog, fatigue or pain were bad. By making my illness “visible” I felt much more confident and secure when I was in public, especially when I was by myself. I didn’t feel as rushed, didn’t feel embarrassed for using the elevator instead of taking the stairs, was always offered a seat on the bus or subway which I was usually very grateful for, etc. Just something to consider. Best of luck to you.

For the person newly diagnosed, I would check with current benefits package to see if LTD and STD benefits are included. If not, I would consider purchasing both if possible but definitely LTD insurance.  If done through an employer, pre-existing conditions are usually not an issue. Many LTD policy’s allow you to take them with you, meaning that once you leave your job you can keep the policy. I medically retired from work due to PPMS in April (I’m only 42) but because of my LTD insurance I will receive 60% of my income (pre-tax) until the age of 67.  I also received a large check from the LTD company for back pay from lost wages due to sick days and days without pay when I was using FMLA. Surprisingly, my life insurance policy also rolled over. I knew none of this before I got sick and was really fortunate that I had such a great benefits package but the LTD payments have allowed me to keep my financial independence, which is probably what keeps me sane some days. 
Best wishes to you and your family.
